title: Implement the three depth-first traversals of a binary tree — inorder, preorder, and postorder — both recursively and iteratively using an explicit stack.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Inorder/Preorder/Postorder — recursive and iterative (stack)

s1_definition.profdef: The three depth-first traversals differ only in when a node is visited relative to its children. Preorder visits the node before its subtrees, inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and postorder visits both subtrees before the node. Each has a trivially recursive form and an iterative form that uses an explicit stack to simulate the call stack.

In inorder he audits the left team fully, then writes the manager, then audits the right team. In postorder he audits both teams completely before writing the manager last. Same chart, three different orders of recording, chosen depending on what the audit needs.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The three depth-first traversals differ only in when a node is visited relative to its children. Preorder visits the node before its subtrees, inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and postorder visits both subtrees before the node. Each has a trivially recursive form and an iterative form that uses an explicit stack to simulate the call stack.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh audits an org chart three different ways. In preorder he writes down a manager's name first, then audits their teams. In inorder he audits the left team fully, then writes the manager, then audits the right team. In postorder he audits both teams completely before writing the manager last. Same chart, three different orders of recording, chosen depending on what the audit needs.

**One line to remember:** Preorder is node-left-right, inorder is left-node-right, postorder is left-right-node, and the iterative versions replace recursion with an explicit stack.

sections.s2_technical:
All three traversals are depth-first, meaning they go as deep as possible down one branch before backtracking. The only difference is the position of the "visit" relative to the two recursive descents.

The recursive forms are direct translations of the definitions. Preorder: visit the node, then recurse left, then recurse right. For example: `visit(node); preorder(node.left); preorder(node.right);`. Inorder: `inorder(node.left); visit(node); inorder(node.right);`. Postorder: `postorder(node.left); postorder(node.right); visit(node);`. Each has the base case of returning on a null node.

The iterative forms use an explicit stack because recursion is really just the language managing a stack for you. For iterative preorder, you push the root, then pop a node, visit it, and push its right child then its left child, so the left is processed first. For example: `stack.push(root); while(!stack.isEmpty()){ Node n = stack.pop(); visit(n); if(n.right!=null) stack.push(n.right); if(n.left!=null) stack.push(n.left); }`.

Iterative inorder walks left pushing nodes, then pops and visits, then moves right. For example: `while(curr!=null || !stack.isEmpty()){ while(curr!=null){ stack.push(curr); curr=curr.left; } curr=stack.pop(); visit(curr); curr=curr.right; }`.

Iterative postorder is the trickiest; a common trick is to do a modified preorder that visits node-right-left and then reverse the result to get left-right-node. A senior nuance is recognizing that inorder on a binary search tree yields sorted order, which is why inorder is so frequently the right choice for BST problems, and that the iterative forms matter when recursion depth could overflow the stack on very tall trees.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an expression tree represents a fee formula, and the operations team needs it printed in different orders: preorder for a prefix export to another system, inorder to reconstruct the human-readable infix formula, and postorder to feed a stack-based evaluator. This is exactly how the three traversals work — same tree, three output orders.

Problem 2 — Some trees are very tall, and recursion risks a stack overflow, so the team also needs stack-based iterative versions. This is exactly why we implement both recursive and iterative forms.

The mini-project builds an `ExprNode` class, a `TraversalService` with all three recursive and iterative traversals and logging, and a runnable demo over a small fee expression tree.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the expression tree for base plus fee, all times tax, with the multiply at the root.

Step 1: Preorder visits the node first. It records the root multiply, then descends left into plus, records plus, then records base and fee, then returns and records tax. The result is multiply, plus, base, fee, tax, which is the prefix form.

Step 2: Inorder visits the left subtree first. It descends to base and records it, then records plus, then records fee, then records the root multiply, then records tax. The result is base, plus, fee, multiply, tax, which is the human-readable infix order.

Step 3: Postorder visits both subtrees before the node. It records base, then fee, then plus, then tax, then finally the root multiply. The result is base, fee, plus, tax, multiply, which is exactly the postfix order a stack evaluator consumes.

Step 4: The iterative versions produce the identical sequences. Iterative preorder pushes right before left so left is processed first. Iterative inorder walks left pushing nodes, then pops and goes right. Iterative postorder does a node-right-left preorder and reverses it.

```text

2026-10-26T18:10:00Z [INFO] Preorder  (iterative): [*, +, base, fee, tax]
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z [INFO] Inorder   (recursive): [base, +, fee, *, tax]
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z [INFO] Inorder   (iterative): [base, +, fee, *, tax]
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z [INFO] Postorder (recursive): [base, fee, +, tax, *]
2026-10-26T18:10:00Z [INFO] Postorder (iterative): [base, fee, +, tax, *]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Expression tree:         *
                         /   \
                        +     tax
                      /   \
                   base   fee

  Preorder  (N,L,R): *, +, base, fee, tax     → prefix export
  Inorder   (L,N,R): base, +, fee, *, tax     → infix (human)
  Postorder (L,R,N): base, fee, +, tax, *     → postfix (eval)

  Iterative preorder: stack push R then L → pop L first
  Iterative inorder:  push lefts → pop → go right
  Iterative postorder: preorder(N,R,L) then reverse
```

```text
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Recursive DFS (3 orders by visit position)               │
  │  Iterative DFS with explicit stack (simulates call stack) │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   TraversalService                    │
  │  + preorderRecursive/Iterative        │ O(n) each
  │  + inorderRecursive/Iterative         │ inorder on BST = sorted
  │  + postorderRecursive/Iterative       │ postorder = eval order
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Visit position:
    pre  = node, left, right
    in   = left, node, right
    post = left, right, node
  Iterative postorder = (node,right,left) preorder reversed.

  Contract: output order matches the traversal definition.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The three depth-first traversals differ only in one thing: when a node is visited relative to its two children. Preorder visits the node before descending, inorder visits the left subtree then the node then the right subtree, and postorder visits both subtrees before the node. The recursive implementations are direct translations of those definitions with a null base case, which makes them the clearest way to express each order.

The iterative versions matter because recursion is really the language managing a stack on your behalf, and on a very tall tree that implicit stack can overflow. Iterative preorder pushes the root and, on each pop, pushes the right child before the left so the left is processed first. Iterative inorder walks as far left as possible pushing nodes, then pops and visits and moves right. Iterative postorder is the trickiest, and the cleanest trick is to run a modified preorder that visits node, right, then left, and reverse the result to get left, right, node.

The complexity of all six is linear in the number of nodes with space proportional to the height. The single most important property I always mention is that inorder traversal of a binary search tree produces values in sorted order, which is why inorder is the natural choice for so many BST problems.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used these on a fee expression tree. Preorder gave me a prefix export for another system, inorder reconstructed the human-readable infix formula for display, and postorder produced exactly the token order that a stack-based evaluator consumes. Because some formula trees are tall, I kept the iterative stack-based versions alongside the recursive ones so the service never risks a stack overflow in production.
